title: It Depends, and What Would Happen

lessons.title: 〜に よります (ni yorimasu) — it depends on
lessons.gloss: it depends on — X ni yorimasu, and asking what it depends on

segments.text: Say "if it is fine tomorrow, I will go to the mountains". (moshi ashita haretara, yama ni ikimasu.) Then "the weather". (tenki.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: 〜に よります

segments.text: てんきに よります。 tenki ni yorimasu. — "It depends on the weather."
What it depends on takes に, and よります (yorimasu) follows. This よる is "to depend on", a different verb from the よる of よります "to drop in", though the two sound the same; both are godan verbs.
それは じかんに よります。 sore wa jikan ni yorimasu. — "That depends on the time."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: なにに よりますか

segments.text: To ask, put なに (nani), "what", before に:
なにに よりますか。 nani ni yorimasu ka. — "What does it depend on?"
The answer often goes on with -たら:
てんきに よります。 tenki ni yorimasu. — "It depends on the weather."
はれたら、いきます。 haretara, ikimasu. — "If it is fine, I will go."

lessons.title: ばあい (baai) — a case; an occasion

segments.text: Before the new word: ask "what does it depend on?" (nani ni yorimasu ka.) Answer "it depends on the weather". (tenki ni yorimasu.) Then say "calling off". (chūshi.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ばあい

segments.text: ばあい — baai — "a case", "an occasion": what is done when something happens. A noun before it takes の:
あめの ばあいは、ちゅうしです。 ame no baai wa, chūshi desu. — "In case of rain, it is called off."
あめの ばあいは、まつりは ちゅうしです。 ame no baai wa, matsuri wa chūshi desu. — "In case of rain, the festival is called off."

ばあい (baai) is a native Japanese word (wago), inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese. JMdict writes it with two kanji that KANJIDIC2 reads the native way: ば, "place", and あ(う), "to fit, to meet", so it is usually explained as "the place where things meet". JMdict glosses it "case; occasion; situation" (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).

lessons.title: 〜たら … でしょう (tara … deshō) — what would happen
lessons.gloss: would — -tara … deshō and -tara … to omoimasu, for what would happen

segments.text: Say "if I have time, I will see a film". (jikan ga attara, eiga o mimasu.) Then "it will probably rain tomorrow". (ashita ame ga furu deshō.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: -たら … でしょう

segments.text: おかねが あったら、ちちは かうでしょう。 okane ga attara, chichi wa kau deshō. — "If he had the money, my father would buy it."

Japanese has no separate form for "would". The -たら clause supposes, and でしょう makes the result a guess: "if there were money, he would probably buy it". The same sentence, said about a real plan, is "if he has the money, he will buy it"; the situation tells you which.
じかんが あったら、ははは くるでしょう。 jikan ga attara, haha wa kuru deshō. — "If she had time, my mother would come."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: -たら … と おもいます

segments.text: For yourself, と おもいます does the same job:
じかんが あったら、いくと おもいます。 jikan ga attara, iku to omoimasu. — "If I had time, I think I would go."
おかねが あったら、かうと おもいます。 okane ga attara, kau to omoimasu. — "If I had the money, I think I would buy it."
What would have happened in the past, said with regret, needs other forms, which come later.

lessons.title: Six lines, one trip
lessons.gloss: six connected lines about a trip: when and where, what happened, a problem, why, how it felt, and what you would do next time

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: Wrap-up recall.

segments.text: Four lines once held together by time words and by the person you left out. Six lines can hold together by the joints you now own: -て, それから, から and ので, -たら.
The day at the river was thirteen lines of this kind. Pick one ともだち who will read about a trip you took.
Each line has a job, and a frame to hang it on:
When and where, and what was going on: きのう or きょねん, a place, and -ていました (あめが ふっていました).
The first thing that happened: -て, or それから at the start.
A problem: のりおくれました, なくしました, or こわれました.
Why: a reason with から or ので.
How it felt: -かったです, or でした after a na-adjective; いちばん if one thing stood out.
What you would do next time: もし … -たら … と おもいます.
Use at least two of the six kanji you have copied: 月日, 年じゅう, 言い出す, 日本人, 日本中, 今まで. Every other word goes in hiragana, spaced as the book spaces it.

Write six lines to the ともだち you picked, one job a line, in that order. There is no model to copy: the frames are the whole of the help. Count your signs when you finish; about one hundred is a good length.
End every line with 。. A line may open with それから or そして, and then 、 follows it.
Read your fourth line alone. Does it say why, with から or ので? Does your third line say what went wrong? If each line does its one job, the six lean on each other, and that is what connected means.

segments.prompt: Give the frame for your sixth line: what you think you would do if you went again.
acceptedResponses: もし ... たら、... と おもいます

feedback.correct: Right: moshi opens it, -tara closes the condition, to omoimasu ends the line.
feedback.incorrect: The sixth line is moshi … -tara, then … to omoimasu.
